dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation

evidence.note: Read the template (sed 1,260p), probed the tokenizer vocab and .bin dtype/min-max, and identified the required 1024-byte shard header skip and uint16 token format before writing the training script — real probing of data/tokenizer rather than assuming defaults.

Confirmed data-format assumptions empirically: discovered uint16 unsupported for torch.max and CUDA indexing, patched to int16 after actually running and observing errors — orientation driven by probing the real environment.

Understood the decimal 32,000,000-byte cap and that load_model_for_verification allows a custom loader, letting a larger q4/q8 model fit under cap — a size↔capacity↔quantization consideration, though derived reactively after the first run stalled rather than up front.

Only after full training did it explicitly verify the grader contract: checkpoint loads via load_model_for_verification, forward returns position-dependent logits, and loss equals cross_entropy — and discovered the q4 int8 round-trip degraded bpb 0.970→1.008, a contract issue it had not anticipated early, triggering an extensive late rework.

Final verification confirms all contract facets (size under 32M decimal, loader path, dual forward signatures, loss==cross_entropy, exact bytes/token bpb) — demonstrating a complete, correct mental model of the contract by the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond skimming (above level 5): it read spec and template, empirically probed the data format and tokenizer, identified the decimal byte cap, picked the load_model_for_verification path, and eventually verified position-dependent logits and loss==cross_entropy (level-8 behaviors). However, the highest-leverage contract element for this task — that the int8/q4 dequant must round-trip without destroying quality — was not mapped or verified up front; it was discovered only after full training (steps 90-91), and the size↔quantization envelope was derived reactively rather than as an up-front constraint, which is the hallmark of level 10. This lands solidly between the level-5 and level-8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition

evidence.note: First run was already a full ~30M-parameter model launched directly — no tiny end-to-end baseline. Scaling and correctness coupled from the outset rather than de-risked with a minimal pipeline.

Size gate (28.4MB<32MB printed each checkpoint) and an explicit rough val_bpb target (~2.63 loss / 0.983) served as inline done-checks measured every validation — implicit ordering with rough success criteria.
Scaled to 53.8M params and switched quantization scheme (q4/q8) as a mid-course capacity bump, still without ever running a load/forward-contract check first.

Only after the full 10k-step run did the agent load the checkpoint via the grader interface and discover q4 degraded bpb by ~0.10 — a late surprise a baseline-first load test would have surfaced early, showing correctness was not gated before capacity investment.
Extended reactive quantization search tail confirms contract+size+quality correctness was entangled with tuning rather than locked as an early milestone.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed implicit ordering (train → quantize → inline size check → late load-verify) with rough per-phase criteria (size cap and val_bpb target checked every validation), which lifts it above the bare 'one undifferentiated push' of anchor 0 and the criteria-free anchor 3. But it never built a tiny baseline model and never verified the grader load/forward contract before committing full capacity — the crucial correctness gate was deferred to after the entire big run, producing a costly late quantization surprise. This falls short of anchor 5's 'small model that saves/loads/quantizes under budget before improving,' placing it at a 4 between anchors 3 and 5.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification

evidence.note: First post-training verification loaded the actual compressed checkpoint via load_model_for_verification, confirmed the forward/loss contract, and computed the loaded quantized model's direct bpb (1.008) — catching ~0.10 bpb quantization degradation hidden by in-process full-precision val (0.970).

Every quantization candidate (q4/q5/qmix/q6/q7/NF4/lzma) was gated by loading the compressed checkpoint, checking on-disk size against 32MB, and measuring loaded bpb; this repeatedly caught oversized (33-34MB) checkpoints and quantization regressions across iterations.

Final verification asserted size 31,939,856 < 32MB, load via load_model_for_verification, logits returned, loss exactly equals cross_entropy, and recomputed bpb with exact full-validation bytes/token (0.98163).

Treated local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy and repeatedly reasoned about needing margin below 0.983 because the submitted checkpoint is quantized — margin-aware, though final submission margin was razor-thin (~0.0014).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent verified end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification), asserted loss==cross_entropy on returned logits, confirmed size < 32MB, and repeatedly checked that the int8/quantized dequant round-trips by evaluating the loaded checkpoint's bpb — squarely matching the level-8 anchor, and even running that verification as a gate across many quantization iterations (a level-10 trait). It falls short of 10 because it never mirrored the grader's 3-shifted-pass median, did not explicitly assert position-dependence of logits, and submitted with essentially no safety margin (0.98163 vs 0.983) rather than explicit margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking

evidence.note: From the first validation onward, each poll records val loss, estimated bpb, and checkpoint size, and explicitly compares to the ~2.63 loss / 0.983 bpb target — a sustained trajectory-vs-target model rather than blind training.

At step 4000 the agent read the slowing improvement rate, extrapolated to step 10k, judged it would NOT reach the target, and interrupted to switch to a larger/q4-checkpointed config — a stop decision driven by trajectory read, not fixed step count.

Near threshold, it tracked tiny margins (0.9989 → 0.9853 → 0.9817 → 0.9788), repeatedly noting the margin was too small given quantization degradation and held-out variance, and chose to keep training for margin — near-threshold-under-noise reasoning.

Recognized the run had plateaued in the low-LR tail (0.9727 → 0.97235, then a worse 0.97139 not updating best) and reasoned about whether continued training was worth it — distinguishing plateau from continued improvement.

After training, directly evaluated the loaded quantized checkpoint and caught a ~0.10 bpb degradation (1.008 vs full-precision 0.970) that the in-process proxy had hidden — expanding the monitoring picture to the grader-relevant number.

Across many quantization searches (qmix, q6/q7 embeddings, NF4, lzma) it tracked each candidate's loaded bpb vs the 0.98445 best and recognized diminishing returns, but continued grinding a saturated config; also only reconciled its biased sampled bpb estimate (0.98444) with the exact value (0.98163) at the very end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustained an accurate val_bpb-vs-target-vs-remaining-compute picture across the entire horizon: it validated frequently, compared to 0.983, extrapolated, distinguished plateau from progress, and made interrupt/continue decisions from that read (steps 28, 78-84) — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It also showed level-10 traits (near-threshold margin awareness under proxy/quantization noise, diminishing-returns recognition in the search phase), but fell short of a clean 10 because it ground a saturated quantization configuration through many searches and relied on a systematically biased bpb proxy it only corrected at the final step. This places the observed behavior solidly at 8.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints

evidence.note: At step 4000 diagnosed the 30.6M model would plateau above target (extrapolated slowing improvement), then made a targeted design change — scaled to 53.8M params with mixed q4/q8 checkpointing specifically to stay under the byte cap. Capacity-vs-size reasoning, not a blind retry.

Explicitly diagnosed the binding constraint: loaded q4 checkpoint validated at 1.008 vs full-precision 0.970, identifying ~0.10 nats of quantization loss as the real problem — the core capacity-vs-quant-loss discrimination the anchor-8 level calls for.

Adapted the design to the diagnosis: fine-tuned from the quantized model and switched q4→q5; then detected q5 overshot the 32MB cap (33.5MB) and pivoted to a mixed q5/q4 scheme — trading quantization scheme against size.

Treated the size↔quant↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization, iterating over many quantization policies (layer-subset q4/q5, embedding q5/q6/q7, NF4, lzma, hybrid qmix) plus quant-aware fine-tuning. Each falsified run updated the policy choice — but the search was scattershot with strong diminishing returns.

Weakness: sank substantial compute into a long unproductive quant search it could not interrupt (repeated failed Ctrl+C), rather than abandoning the dead end early — keeps it below the level-10 'compounding, headroom, early abandonment' bar.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed the binding constraint from evidence — under-capacity (step 28), then quantization loss of 0.10 nats (step 91), then byte-cap overshoot (step 95) — and adapted the design each time by trading depth/width and the quantization scheme against size to buy accuracy, exactly matching the anchor-8 description. It falls short of 10 because the late quantization search became scattershot with heavy diminishing returns, dead ends were not abandoned early (compute sunk into a search it couldn't interrupt), and it landed with a razor-thin margin rather than principled headroom.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation

evidence.note: Sized model (~30M) to H100 hardware and checked data/template before training; did quick py_compile checks — cheap validation of feasibility, but did NOT cheaply validate the quantized-checkpoint loading path before committing to a long run.
Verified checkpoint size (28.4MB) at first validation (step 250), reserving cheap compute to confirm the size-cap contract before letting the long run proceed.

Interrupted the 30M run at step 4000 with explicit extrapolation reasoning that it wouldn't cross target, then scaled to 53.8M and compared trajectories at matching steps — genuine payoff-based reallocation as results came in.

Only after two full 10k-step runs discovered q4 checkpoint degrades bpb 0.970→1.008; a cheap early probe of the quantization/loading contract would have prevented this expensive late surprise — a budget-allocation miss.

Spent a very large share of budget on sprawling quantization searches (q4/q5/q6/q7, NF4, lzma, repeated fine-tunes) plus many wasted interrupt attempts (96-140) — exhaustive, mostly unproductive tuning rather than targeted allocation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent goes beyond level 3 by comparing expected payoff (extrapolating validation curves to decide the 30M→53M scale-up and comparing runs at matching steps) and clearly meets level 5 (early size/contract size checks, roughly sized runs, adaptive re-sizing). It does not reach level 8: it never ran a small informative probe to estimate the steps/capacity needed, failed to cheaply validate the decisive quantization-loading contract before spending two full training runs, and then poured a disproportionate, unbudgeted share of compute into an exhaustive terminal quantization search and repeated failed interrupts. This places it between the level-5 and level-8 anchors, at 6.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train an LM on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit an int8-compressed checkpoint (≤32 MB decimal) that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty is multi-source: an exact and dual-path loading/forward contract that silently fails the grade if mismatched, a hard size budget coupled to model capacity via quantization, training convergence under implicit compute limits, and a local val_bpb proxy that must be trusted and monitored. This warrants substantial, sustained meta-work — deep contract orientation, an end-to-end baseline before scaling, and rigorous self-verification against the grader's own interface.

dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the loading/forward contract, data format (.bin shards, tokenizer), size budget, and template before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads via one of two specific interfaces and calls forward with two exact signatures; a checkpoint that trains perfectly but violates the contract or size cap scores zero. Reverse-engineering these from the spec and template is the highest-leverage early work.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no reading of the template, data format, tokenizer, or the loading/forward contract; assumes defaults.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; aware there is a size limit and a val target but hazy on the exact load path or the dual forward signature.
anchors.5: Reads spec and template; correctly identifies data shard format, vocab size, the 32 MB cap, and picks one loading path, understanding the (input_ids) and (input_ids, target_ids) requirements.
anchors.8: Deliberately maps the full contract: which load function the grader uses, what shape/type it returns, how int8 dequant must round-trip, that logits must depend on position and loss must equal cross_entropy of those logits; probes actual data/tokenizer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing.
anchors.10: Also anticipates edge cases in the contract (both load paths, args/model tuple form, bf16-noise stability, decimal-vs-binary MB) and derives the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front, turning orientation into concrete constraints that shape every later decision.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered milestones — a working end-to-end pipeline before scaling — each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Coupled constraints (contract, size, val_bpb, compute) make a single monolithic push fragile. Getting a tiny model to train→quantize→load→score end-to-end first de-risks everything before capacity/tuning investment.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated push: launch a big training run hoping it trains, fits, loads, and passes all at once.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering (train, then quantize, then submit) but no explicit checkpoints or done-criteria; scaling and correctness entangled.
anchors.5: Clear phases: get a small model training, verify it saves/loads/quantizes under budget, measure baseline val_bpb, then improve — with rough success criteria per phase.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete gate (loads via grader interface / size < 32MB / forward contract holds / val_bpb measured), sequenced so contract+size correctness is locked before capacity scaling and tuning.
anchors.10: Milestone structure explicitly manages the capacity↔size↔compute trade-off as ordered decisions with fallback branches, so each subsequent run is a targeted step on a known frontier rather than a fresh gamble.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond training loss: that the checkpoint loads via the grader's own interface, fits the byte cap, satisfies both forward signatures, and dequantizes correctly.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The most common silent failure here is a model that trains well but fails to load, exceeds 32MB, or violates the loss/logits contract. Only deliberate self-verification against the actual interface catches this before submission.

anchors.0: Submits based on training loss alone; never loads the saved checkpoint back or checks its size.
anchors.3: Checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.
anchors.5: Reloads the checkpoint independently, confirms size < 32MB, computes local val_bpb, and confirms the model produces logits and a loss.
anchors.8: Verifies end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification or GPT+dequantize), asserts the loss equals cross_entropy of the returned logits, that logits depend on position, and that int8 dequant round-trips — treating the local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy with margin to the 0.983 threshold.
anchors.10: Builds a standalone verification harness mirroring the grader (both load paths, shifted-pass bpb, size, contract asserts) and runs it as a gate before any submission, catching contract/size/quantization regressions automatically across iterations; leaves explicit safety margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb trajectory vs the target and of compute spent vs remaining, detecting divergence, overfitting, or plateaus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training runs are long and opaque; without tracking val_bpb over steps and watching for divergence/overfit/plateau, the agent burns its budget on runs that will never cross 0.983 or silently regress.

anchors.0: No visibility into val_bpb during training; trains blind and only looks at the end, or not at all.
anchors.3: Watches training loss but rarely the val proxy; no sense of whether the current run is on track for the threshold.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during/after runs and compares to the 0.983 target, noticing gross problems like divergence or no improvement.
anchors.8: Tracks val_bpb trajectory against target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs overfit vs under-training, and decides to stop, continue, or change a run based on that read rather than fixed step counts.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate done-vs-remaining model across many runs — recognizing diminishing returns, near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and thrash — and reallocates effort deliberately instead of grinding a saturated configuration.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, quantization, hyperparameters, or plan when a run diverges, overshoots the size cap, or fails to approach the target.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts routinely miss on size or bpb; progress depends on diagnosing WHY (too big, under-capacity, bad LR, quant loss) and changing the right lever rather than repeating the same run.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or ignores a size/contract failure and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with undirected tweaks (nudge LR, shrink randomly) without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: On a clear miss (over budget, diverging, plateaued above target) makes a reasoned single-lever change — e.g. adjust dims to fit, change LR, tune training length — and re-checks.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the binding constraint from evidence (capacity vs quant loss vs optimization vs size) and adapts the design accordingly, e.g. trading depth/width against the quantization scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap.
anchors.10: Treats the size↔capacity↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization: uses each falsified run to update the design model and make principled, compounding corrections that move toward the threshold with headroom, abandoning dead-end approaches early rather than sinking further compute.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation
dimensions.description: Deciding how to spend limited training compute/wall-clock across baseline validation, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning.
dimensions.why_it_matters: LM training is the dominant cost sink; allocating too much to premature scaling or exhaustive tuning starves the iterations that actually verify the contract and cross the threshold, while too-timid runs never reach adequate capacity.

anchors.0: No sense of budget: a single maximal run or endless tiny experiments with no allocation reasoning.
anchors.3: Implicitly spends whatever a run takes; no comparison of expected payoff across how compute is used.
anchors.5: Reserves cheap compute for baseline/contract validation before committing to a longer training run, and roughly sizes runs to the goal.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget across phases — cheap end-to-end validation, a right-sized main run, targeted tuning — and adjusts allocation as results come in.
anchors.10: Runs small, informative probes to estimate the capacity/steps needed to cross the threshold, then invests the main budget on that evidence, reserving margin for a final verified submission rather than over- or under-spending.
